President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, In my capacity as Chair of the Expert Mechanism on the Right to Development, it is an honour to present to this Council our annual report, along with two thematic studies prepared by my fellow experts. Since our last report to this Council, the Expert Mechanism held its 12th session in Geneva from the 27th to the 29th of October 2025. It also held its 13th session in New York from the 21st to the 23rd of April 2026. At our 12th session, we convened five focused thematic discussions on the impacts of trade tariffs on the realization of the right to development, on the impact of artificial intelligence on creative industries and cultural rights, on the role of civil society organizations in realizing the right to development at the grassroots level, on public participation as a tool for development, and on the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development. At our 13th session, we held further thematic discussions and substantive debates addressing, among other topics, artificial intelligence, peace and security, the role of regional mechanisms, equality and non-discrimination, the draft International Covenant on the Right to Development, and the participation and inclusion of migrants in development processes. We are grateful for the proactive engagement of Member States and UN entities, as well as intergovernmental organizations, regional mechanisms, national human rights institutions, academia, non-governmental organizations, and other stakeholders throughout both sessions. President, as we present this report, we feel it may be useful to recall the particular contribution that the expert mechanism seeks to make to the work of this Council. Our mandate is to provide the Council with thematic expertise on the right to development, to search for, identify and share best practices with Member States, and to promote the implementation of the right to development worldwide. This mandate is carried out through our annual sessions, thematic studies, study visits, contributions to international processes, and interactive discussions and consultations with Member States, UN entities, regional mechanisms, national human rights institutions, academia and civil society. It is in this spirit that today we present two thematic studies before this Council. These studies identify best practices and recommendations to advance the implementation of the right to development in relation to two pressing global challenges. These thematic studies, who are prepared by former members of the mechanism, are climate finance, vulnerability and responsibility, and artificial intelligence, cultural rights and the right to development. They are contained in documents A/HRC/63/39 and A/HRC/63/40, respectively. The first study looks at climate finance through the lens of vulnerability and responsibility. It calls for climate financing that is grounded in equality, meaningful participation, transparency and international co-operation. It takes stock of recent advisory opinions from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the International Court of Justice on climate change, which have clarified and enhanced legal understanding and obligations regarding climate finance. The study examines the potential and the limits of carbon markets, noting risks to their integrity and credibility, including overstated emission reductions and unequal benefit sharing, and calls for robust safeguards, fair pricing, and carbon strategies that are tailored to national contexts, rolled out in phases and supported by international cooperation in order to strengthen the position of least developed countries in carbon markets, while also considering clean cooking initiatives as a further avenue for climate mitigation with direct health and gender benefits. The study further explores critical minerals as a possible source of revenue for producers in developing countries, noting that the right to development and the right to a healthy environment are mutually reinforcing in this sector. It also calls for stronger South-South cooperation among mineral-rich developing countries in the face of recent disruptions to critical mineral supply chains. It also examines the repatriation of illicit financial flows as a means of supporting climate adaptation and transition. Across all these areas, the study finds that equitable benefit sharing and the active, free and meaningful participation of indigenous peoples, local communities and women are preconditions for climate finance to genuinely serve the right to development. The study calls for embedding these principles across climate governance and finance frameworks so that climate finance reflects both current vulnerabilities and the historical responsibility of states for greenhouse gas emissions. The second study examines the implications of artificial intelligence for cultural rights and the right to development. It naturally recognizes AI's potential to broaden access to creative tools, to preserve cultural heritage, and revitalize endangered languages, while at the same time cautioning that without safeguards, It may undermine creativity, displace human creative labor, reproduce dominant cultural and linguistic patterns, and narrow down the space for diverse cultural expression. These risks are especially significant for developing countries. indigenous peoples and minorities, as well as small-scale cultural producers, who all face unequal access to data, infrastructure, markets and decision-making power. The study pays particular attention to the situation of indigenous peoples, whose cultural heritage is increasingly used to train AI systems, at times without their free, prior and informed consent. It describes this practice as a form of what it terms digital extractivism, and it calls for the recognition of indigenous data sovereignty, community-based data governance, and equitable benefit sharing arrangements. The study recommends that AI governance be grounded in international human rights law and shaped by the right to development, so that it supports inclusive, culturally diverse, and human-centered development, rather than cultural homogenization and the concentration of creative and technological power It also calls for effective accountability and access to remedy for affected communities. The study further calls on states to adopt robust regulatory frameworks, ensuring transparency and human oversight, to reform intellectual property regimes in order to protect creators' interests, and to invest in multilingual data infrastructure. It calls on businesses and business enterprises to conduct human rights due diligence and to ensure transparency in their use of training data. In line with the Declaration on the Right to Development, the study also calls for strengthened international cooperation through technology transfer, capacity building and financial assistance. We trust that both studies will be of practical use to Member States and other stakeholders in advancing the right to development, and we look forward to continuing to draw on your inputs as we work to finalise our forthcoming study on peace, security and the right to development, which is expected in 2027. President, the liquidity situation affecting the United Nations regular budget has had direct and concrete consequences for the implementation of our mandate this year, including the cancellation of mandated country study visits and contributions to international processes. It has also included reduced opportunities for the participation of expert guests in our sessions. Despite these constraints, we have continued to engage with Member States and other stakeholders, including through side events and the development of policy briefs designed to make our thematic studies more accessible to a wider audience. This year's 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development is, for the Expert Mechanism, much more than an occasion for commemoration. It is an opportunity to renew political commitment to this right and to translate the principles set out in 1986 into specific action and effective implementation. We also see it as an opportunity to build greater momentum towards the adoption of a draft International Covenant on the Right to Development. Looking ahead, the Expert Mechanism intends to build on this work by finalizing our study on peace, security and the right to development, and by considering, among possible future themes proposed by our newly appointed members, illicit financial flows, indigenous peoples and self-determined development, an adequate standard of living, and the impact of mandatory corporate human rights due diligence legislation on the right to development. We will also continue to deepen our engagement with regional mechanisms and with civil society at grassroots level. We are also preparing for our 14th session, which is to be held in Geneva from the 26th to the 28th of October 2026, and we would welcome very much your active participation in that session. I look forward to our interactive dialogue and to your guidance on the effective implementation of the mandate of our mechanism. Thank you very much for your attention.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, representatives of civil society, colleagues and friends. It is an honor to address the Human Rights Council for the first time as United Nations Rapporteur on Toxics and Human Rights. I take up this mandate at a time when the scale and complexity of toxic pollution is increasing rapidly, impacting human rights. Chemicals and hazardous materials move through and into our economies and environments, from extraction and production to transportation, use, waste, and remediation. They enter our air, water, soil, food, and ultimately our bodies, and they impact the enjoyment of many, if not all, human rights. These consequences are not equally distributed. Workers, women, children, indigenous peoples, people of African descent, persons in poverty, people living in frontline and fence line communities are exposed first and worst. At its core, this mandate asks how we can ensure that the extraction, production, and use of chemicals meet all three pillars of sustainability, ecological, social, and economic. And how can we strengthen evidence-based approaches to protecting human rights? Excellencies, today I present two reports of my predecessor, Dr. Marcos Oriana. The thematic report, Forever Chemicals and Human Rights, and the report on his country visit to Mexico. The thematic report examines per- and perfluoralkyl substances, called PFAS. through a human rights perspective. PFAS are thousands of synthetic chemicals that are highly persistent and travel long distances through air and water. Once released, they may remain in the environment for centuries, and there are currently no effective and scalable technologies capable of removing PFAS from contaminated ecosystems. Exposure occurs across the full life cycle at production sites and occupational settings, through contaminated water, food, and in consumer products. PFAS impair rights, including the right to life, to health, to a healthy environment, to a safe and healthy working environment, and access to information, justice, and remedy. They can cross the placenta. They've been found in the blood of umbilical cords, in breast milk. They expose people at their most sensitive developmental stages. Exposure can also affect our hormone systems, our liver function, our immune systems. So this is an issue of global environmental justice. These are largely manufactured in industrial states and spread globally through emissions, through transboundary movement of PFAS-laden waste. Communities that are already facing poverty, discrimination, and marginalization often carry a disproportionate share of the consequences. The report underlines the human rights obligations of governments to prevent toxic exposures and calls for urgent action, including an immediate ban on all non-essential uses. Its message is fundamentally one of prevention. When pollution is highly persistent and potentially irreversible, Waiting for complete certainty before acting can itself cause harm. On the country visit to Mexico, I join my predecessor in thanking the government of Mexico for its excellent cooperation and the many communities, civil society representatives, public authorities, academics, and others who shared their experiences and knowledge. The report recognizes Mexico's important international environmental leadership and constitutional recognition of the rights to health and to a healthy environment. It also identifies serious challenges, including sacrifice zones, hazardous pesticides, agro-industrial practices, mercury mining, industrial and water pollution, and obstacles to access to information, participation, justice, and effective remedy. The proliferation of industrialization and sacrifice zones is of particular concern, and the report calls for stronger environmental governance, standards based in the best available science, effective enforcement, meaningful participation, access to information, and protection for human rights defenders. And finally, I would like to take this opportunity to address my vision. As I begin my tenure, I would like to allow how I will approach my mandate. I come to this role as a professor of environmental toxic science and ecotoxicology. My professional life has been devoted to understanding how hazardous chemicals move through ecosystems and the consequences of exposure from molecular toxicity to planetary scale impacts. Toxics introduce multiple dimensions of harm across their full life cycle, and we cannot continue to manage toxic pollution primarily after harm has occurred. We must move upstream, and this will be central to my mandate. Moving upstream means looking across the full life cycle. It means asking not only how we can clean up contamination, but asking why hazardous substances enter into our products, our bodies, our economies in the first place, whether their uses are essential, and whether safer and more sustainable alternatives exist. It means taking up a holistic, integrated approach and looking across sectors to prevent harms from spanning across multiple domains. It means applying precaution where there's credible evidence for potentially serious, irreversible harm. Human rights protections cannot wait decades for certainty while harm continues. My second priority would be strengthening the interface between science and human rights. People cannot protect themselves from risks they do not know about. States cannot form effective policies without reliable evidence. Courts cannot provide justice when essential information on toxics remains unavailable to them. We must protect independent science from conflicts of interest, disinformation, and manufactured doubt, while supporting scientific progress and making knowledge accessible to those whose rights are at stake. Third, global environmental justice will remain at the heart of this mandate. Those carrying the greatest toxic burdens are often those with the least power to determine their living and working conditions. A human rights-based approach requires us to ask not how much pollution exists, but who is poisoned and who benefits, who bears the costs, and who makes the rules. Prevention requires accountability. States have obligations to protect human rights. Businesses have responsibilities to respect them. Where harm occurs, people must have access to information, meaningful participation, justice, and effective remedy. Finally, I want to make this a mandate that bridges and connects. Scientific expertise is indispensable, but it is not sufficient. Workers understand workplace exposures. Communities understand changes in their water, their land, their health. Indigenous peoples hold knowledge that is accumulated across generations. Civil society, health professionals, scientists, and other knowledge holders see dimensions of problems that can otherwise remain invisible. I therefore intend to build strong dialogue across scientific disciplines, regions, forms of knowledge, connecting science, human rights, public health, policy, and lived experiences. Excellencies, toxic pollution is sometimes presented as an inevitable price of development, but I reject that premise. Science can help us identify harm. Human rights can tell us why that harm matters and whose rights must be protected and where the responsibilities lie. The knowledge and experience of affected people can help us understand what meaningful solutions require. Ultimately, our task is not to manage hazardous substances more effectively. It is to ensure that people everywhere can live, work, study, play, and raise generations in a toxic-free environment. I thank you for your attention, and I look forward to our dialogue.
